description: This dataset provides 28 years of environmental monitoring data (1995–2023) from 51 stations in the estuaries and coastal areas of the Basque Country in the Bay of Biscay. Covering 130 variables across water, sediments, and biota, it includes detailed records of phytoplankton, macroalgae, macroinvertebrates, and fish. Compiled in collaboration with the Basque Water Agency (URA), the dataset supports analysis of environmental responses to human pressures and management interventions, identifying patterns of environmental quality improvement within a context of natural variability. Provided in a FAIR² Data Package, the dataset is structured to ensure Findability, Accessibility, Interoperability, Reusability, and Artificial Intelligence-readiness, facilitated by structured metadata and Application Programming Interface access. This resource is intended for researchers and policymakers examining anthropogenic and natural influences on aquatic ecosystems, contributing to sustainable management, conservation practices, and alignment with European directives, including the Water Framework Directive.

methodSection.description: The study was designed to monitor and analyze long-term environmental trends in the Basque Country’s marine ecosystems, focusing on water quality, sediment characteristics, and biological communities. The approach involved systematic sampling across multiple sites and taxa groups, employing standardized protocols to ensure data consistency and reliability over the nearly three-decade period. This methodology facilitated the assessment of anthropogenic impacts and the effectiveness of management interventions, providing a comprehensive understanding of ecosystem dynamics in response to both human activities and natural variability.
methodSection.name: Research Design and Approach

step.name: Objective and Scope
step.description: The primary objective of this study was to assess environmental quality trends in the Basque Country’s marine ecosystems using long-term monitoring data from 1995 to 2023. Key areas of interest include examining water, sediment, and biological components to understand the impact of human pressures, such as industrial and urban discharges, as well as the effectiveness of management actions, like wastewater treatment. This dataset, gathered from 70 sampling stations across the Bay of Biscay, provides insights into environmental changes, supporting the overarching hypothesis that implemented management actions yield positive ecological effects.

step.name: Approach Overview
step.description: The study utilized an observational monitoring approach, gathering data over nearly three decades to facilitate trend analysis on ecosystem variables affected by anthropogenic and natural factors. Sampling followed standardized protocols for various ecosystems (water, sediment, and biota), as outlined by the Basque Water Agency (URA) and AZTI. Data collection methodologies, including EN 15972:2011 guidelines for water quality sampling, were consistently applied to enable cross-temporal and spatial comparisons. Detailed sampling protocols can be found in the URA resource portal: https://www.uragentzia.euskadi.eus/informacion/protocolos-de-muestreo-de-laboratorio-y-de-calculo-de-indices-y-metricas-para-el-seguimiento-del-estado-de-las-masas-de-agua-superficial-de-la-capv/webura00-01040102seguimiento/es/

methodSection.name: Instrumentation and Sample Preparation

step.name: Taxa Group and Sampling Protocols

substep.name: Water
substep.description: Water was sampled every three months, and monthly at a few stations: surface water was collected with a Niskin bottle for nutrients and contaminants, and a CTD was used for temperature, salinity, depth, irradiance, chlorophyll, light transmission, pH and dissolved oxygen.

substep.name: Sediments
substep.description: Sediments were sampled annually in winter (January to March), with a 0.1 m2 van Veen grab at coastal stations and a 0.03 m2 grab at the estuarine station E-A10. Each sample was frozen until laboratory analysis.

substep.name: Biota
substep.description: Sampling was tailored to each biological group: macroinvertebrates annually in winter, phytoplankton quarterly, macroalgae in spring or early summer every three years, and demersal fish and crustaceans in autumn by beam trawl.

step.description: Sampling methodologies were tailored to each group (taxagroup) to ensure accurate and representative data collection.

step.name: Instrumentation and References
step.description: Instruments such as van Veen grabs, CTD sensors, and beam trawls were utilized. Calibration and handling followed standardized protocols where available. Key references, including EN 15972:2011 and URA guidelines, were applied to ensure consistency. Detailed protocols are accessible at the URA resource portal: https://www.uragentzia.euskadi.eus/informacion/protocolos-de-muestreo-de-laboratorio-y-de-calculo-de-indices-y-metricas-para-el-seguimiento-del-estado-de-las-masas-de-agua-superficial-de-la-capv/webura00-01040102seguimiento/es/

step.name: Setup of Tools/Systems

substep.name: Water Sampling
substep.description: Surface water was collected with a Niskin bottle and profiled in situ with a CTD, following EN 15972:2011 and the URA sampling protocols.

substep.name: Sediment Sampling
substep.description: Subtidal sediments were collected with van Veen grabs (0.1 m2 coastal, 0.03 m2 estuarine); intertidal estuarine stations were sampled with a 0.5 x 0.5 m quadrat to 15 cm depth.

substep.name: Biota Sampling
substep.description: Demersal fauna were sampled with beam trawls - 1.5 m wide (10 mm mesh, 8 mm cod end) in the smaller estuaries and 2.5 m wide (40 mm mesh, 14 mm cod end) in the Nerbioi - towed for 10 minutes at 1.5 knots. Macroalgae were sampled along intertidal transects with quadrats, and macroinvertebrate replicates were sieved through a 1 mm mesh.

step.description: Instrumentation and sampling setups varied by component, adhering to standardized protocols across water, sediment, and biota sampling.

step.name: Calibration of Instruments
step.description: Calibration applied to the instruments used across the monitoring programme. It is documented in detail for the CTD sensor; calibration records for the van Veen grab and the beam trawl were not available in the source documentation.

step.name: Apply and document all additional calibration protocols.
step.description: Apply and document all additional calibration protocols.

step.name: CTD Calibration
step.description: The CTD sensor used in water sampling underwent regular calibration to ensure accuracy in measurements of dissolved oxygen, temperature, and salinity, following EN 15972:2011 protocols for water quality. Calibration details for sediment and biota equipment, such as the van Veen grab or beam trawl, were not documented in the provided information.

step.name: Sample Preparation

substep.name: Water Samples
substep.description: Water collected for nutrient and contaminant determination was handled under the applicable ISO and EN 15972:2011 standards; CTD readings were taken in situ and required no preparation.

substep.name: Sediment Samples
substep.description: Sediment samples were frozen on collection and held frozen until laboratory analysis.

substep.name: Biota Samples
substep.description: Macroinvertebrate replicates were sieved through a 1 mm mesh and preserved in formaldehyde until identification under a stereomicroscope. Trawled fish and crustaceans were identified onboard and released.

step.description: Sample preparation varied by component type, based on the specific parameter and storage requirements.

methodSection.description: Equipment used for each component and the handling of samples between collection and laboratory analysis: Niskin bottles and a CTD for water, van Veen grabs and quadrats for sediments and intertidal biota, and beam trawls for demersal fauna, with calibration and preparation following the URA protocols and EN 15972:2011.

methodSection.name: Data Collection

step.name: Sampling Frequency and Timing
step.description:
Sampling was conducted on the following schedules:
- **Water**: Quarterly, with some stations sampled at both high and low tides.
- **Sediments**: Annually, during January.
- **Phytoplankton** and Macroalgae: Quarterly.
- **Fish and Invertebrates**: Seasonal, aligned with site accessibility and species-specific behavior.

step.name: Temporal Data Logging
step.description: Collection dates (datecollected) were systematically recorded for all components to ensure robust temporal analyses.

step.name: Timing and Frequency

substep.name: Water
substep.description: Quarterly, with some stations sampled at both high and low tides and a few sampled monthly.

substep.name: Sediments
substep.description: Annually, in January, within the winter sampling window of January to March.

substep.name: Biota
substep.description: Phytoplankton and macroalgae quarterly; fish and invertebrates seasonally, aligned with site accessibility and species-specific behaviour.

step.description: Data collection followed a consistent schedule, ensuring reliable comparisons over time.

step.name: Variables and Measurements

substep.name: Water Variables
substep.description: Water measurements are held in the WATER record set as parameter, parameter_value and parameter_standardunit triples, keyed by collection date, station and sample and qualified by sampling depth and effort.

substep.name: Sediment Variables
substep.description: Sediment measurements are held in the Sediments record set on the same parameter, parameter_value and parameter_standardunit model, qualified by sampling depth and effort.

substep.name: Biota Variables
substep.description: Biological measurements are held in the Biota, Phytoplankton, Macroalgae, Invertebrates and Fish record sets, which add taxaname and taxanameid to the parameter, parameter_value and parameter_standardunit triple.

step.description: Explicitly measured variables were selected to provide a comprehensive view of environmental quality across components.

step.name: Data Logging and Monitoring
step.description:
Data logging procedures ensured systematic tracking for each component.
- Real-time logging was applied for immediate on-site measurements like temperature, dissolved oxygen, and pH. For sediment and biota samples, data were logged upon completion of laboratory analysis.
- The documentation did not specify whether data logging was performed manually or with automated systems. Information on specific data storage software or data logging methods was also not provided.

methodSection.description: Field collection across the 1995-2023 monitoring programme: the sampling schedule for each component, the recording of collection dates, the variables measured in water, sediments and biota, and how observations were logged.

methodSection.name: Data Processing and Analysis

step.name: Processing of Data

substep.name: Water Data
substep.description: Water records were consolidated into the WATER record set, keyed by collection date, station and sample, with every measurement normalised to a parameter, a value and a standard unit.

substep.name: Sediment and Biota Data
substep.description: Sediment and biota records were consolidated into their record sets on the same parameter, value and standard-unit model, retaining taxon name and identifier for the biological components.

step.description: Data processing involved multiple steps tailored to each component type to ensure consistency and accuracy.

step.name: Post-Processing

substep.name: Trend Analysis
substep.description: Long-term trends were derived per variable across the 1995-2023 series, to assess environmental response to human pressures and to management actions such as wastewater treatment.

substep.name: Software
substep.description: Trend analysis was carried out in R, with non-parametric confidence intervals computed using the boot package. The descriptive statistics published with each record set were generated with pandas.

step.description: After initial processing, data underwent additional statistical analyses to assess long-term environmental trends across variables.

step.name: Analysis Techniques

substep.name: Seasonal Decomposition
substep.description: Series were decomposed into seasonal and trend components, so that long-term change could be separated from the marked seasonal cycle of the monitored variables.

substep.name: Significance Testing
substep.description: Trend significance was assessed non-parametrically, with bootstrap resampling used to derive confidence intervals for each variable.

substep.name: Trend Interpretation
substep.description: Trends were read against the natural variability of each variable, so that improvement attributable to management action could be distinguished from background environmental fluctuation.

step.description: A range of analytical techniques was used to provide robust time-series analyses across variables.

methodSection.description: Consolidation of the raw monitoring records into the published record sets, followed by the statistical analysis used to characterise long-term environmental trends across the monitored variables.

methodSection.name: Quality Assurance and Validation

step.name: Quality Assurance Measures

substep.name: Water Sampling Protocol
substep.description: Water sampling followed EN 15972:2011 and the URA sampling protocols published on the Basque Water Agency resource portal.

substep.name: Sediment and Biota Sampling Protocols
substep.description: Sediment and biota sampling followed the URA protocols for macroinvertebrates, macroalgae and ichthyofauna, applied consistently across stations and years.

substep.name: Instrument Calibration
substep.description: Instruments were calibrated to standardized protocols, the CTD regularly for dissolved oxygen, temperature and salinity under EN 15972:2011.

step.description: Standardized sampling and analytical protocols were followed to ensure data consistency and accuracy.

step.name: Validation Information
step.description: Validation rested on cross-validation against independent datasets where these were available; variables without such a reference were carried forward with the qualifications recorded in the following steps.

step.name: Adjustment for High-Variability Variables
step.description: For variables cross-validated with independent datasets, statistical adjustments were applied to account for environmental variability. These adjustments aimed to refine the trend accuracy by minimizing the influence of natural fluctuations, providing a clearer view of anthropogenic effects.

step.name: Interpretation for High-Variability Variables
step.description: For variables without cross-validation, trends were interpreted with caution. For example, nutrient levels and sediment composition were analyzed with the understanding that observed changes might reflect natural environmental variability in addition to any anthropogenic influence.

step.name: Trend Robustness
step.description: To ensure trend reliability, non-parametric confidence intervals were calculated for each variable using the boot package in R. This approach applied bootstrap resampling to verify trend robustness, particularly for variables where natural variability could impact results.

methodSection.description: Measures taken to keep the 28-year series comparable - standardized sampling and analytical protocols and instrument calibration - together with the treatment of variables whose natural variability limits how far an observed trend can be attributed to human pressure.
